newsitem.title: FINLAND: Nokia, rivals bringing Net to mobiles.
newsitem.headline: Nokia, rivals bringing Net to mobiles.

text.p: European mobile phone giant Nokia Oy said on Monday more of its rivals in the cellular phone industry were backing a joint approach to bringing Internet messages onto mobile handsets.

Nokia, the world's second largest mobile phone maker after the U.S.' Motorola and world number one in digital handsets, said Alcatel, Mitsubishi Electric, Nortel, Philips and Siemens had joined an initiative it set last month with Sweden's Ericsson and Motorola.
"The specification is now being built," said Nokia mobile phones spokeswoman Liisa Nyyssonen. "Basically, it's (about) providing direct access to Internet services from your cellular phone."
Wide industry support for the so-called Wireless Application Protocol may well lead to it becoming an industry standard.

That would mean wireless phone users could gain Internet access no matter what brand their handset. "Nobody wants to end up in a situation where, for example, Nokia phones can get it but not some other," Nyyssonen said.

Standard handset access would let wireless tele-operators distinguish their services through the Internet items they offer. "The operator can decide on the services they perceive as adding value to the customer," Nyyssonen said.

Nokia's Communicator 9000, the first machine of its kind to offer wireless Internet access, makes normal Internet connections. The new joint protocol would involve a network server and data would be based on short message systems.
Smart Messaging Technology, developed by Nokia, currently offers a maximum of 160 characters through routes that do not use radio channels or take up voice capacity.
"There are a whole range of services you can retrieve very, very quickly," Nyyssonen said.

The protocol is initially being developed for GSM (Global Standard for Mobile Communications) digital protocols, which are dominant globally. But Nyyssonen said the aim is also to expand it to include other protocols like CDMA (Code Division Multiple Access), popular in parts of the United States.
